conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You came in with chest pain after trying to eat spinach. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, doc. I was eating spinach and it felt like it got stuck in my throat. I couldn’t swallow it, so I threw up—and right then, I felt this pressure in my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Was the chest pain sharp or dull? Did it go anywhere else, like your arm or jaw?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just pressure, no sharp pain. Didn’t go anywhere. But I’ve had chest pain before, on and off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And how’s your breathing? Any shortness of breath now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m always a little short of breath when I move, but not worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We did an EKG and checked your heart enzymes. Good news—no sign of a heart attack. Your troponin was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why the chest pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be related to your esophagus. You have a history of esophagitis and a stricture, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had trouble swallowing for a couple of weeks now. Thought it was just the usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Swallowing issues plus chest pain after vomiting makes us think the esophagus is involved. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen—no surgical emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no gallbladder or appendix problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, everything looked normal there. But we did see a moderate-to-severe narrowing in one of the arteries to your gut—the SMA. But it’s stable, and you’re not having abdominal pain, so no immediate concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the chest pain now? It’s still there a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it. Your lactate was a bit high earlier, but it’s better now after some fluids. We also did a chest X-ray—some atelectasis in the right lung base, but no pneumonia or fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s atelectasis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means part of the lung is a bit collapsed, common after vomiting or not taking deep breaths. Nothing to treat now, just keep breathing deeply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted GI. Given your history and symptoms, they recommend an upper endoscopy—EGD—to look at your esophagus and possibly dilate the stricture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very safe. We’ll do it tomorrow morning. You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re scheduling your EGD for later today. Any chest pain overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still some pressure, especially when I move my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I pressed on your chest and it reproduced the pain—likely musculoskeletal, maybe from old sternotomy wires. But we’ll still check the esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had that wire pain before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back. The EGD went well. They found severe inflammation and ulcers in your lower esophagus and dilated a 9 mm stricture to 12 mm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I couldn’t swallow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The narrowing was making it hard to pass food. The dilation should help. You’ll need another one in a few weeks to keep it open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more scopes forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we hope not. It depends on how well the esophagus heals and whether the stricture comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching your omeprazole to a dissolving lansoprazole—Prevacid SoluTab. It dissolves under the tongue, easier if you’re having trouble swallowing pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Hemoglobin dipped a bit but not concerning. We’ll keep you on sucralfate and ranitidine for the ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I’m on diltiazem for AFib.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your rhythm has been stable. No AFib episodes. You’ll stay on diltiazem. We didn’t restart blood thinners due to past bleeding, but we’ll discuss that with your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. Chest pain is much better, and you tolerated soft food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your meds, especially the new dissolving Prevacid twice a day. Soft diet for now. No heavy lifting. And schedule your follow-up EGD in about 4 weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using your inhalers—fluticasone and tiotropium. The shortness of breath is likely from COPD, not new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll try to stay off alcohol too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Alcohol can worsen esophagitis and ulcers. We’ll get you connected with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll see you in follow-up soon. Call if chest pain returns or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.
